title: Short Stuff: Hobo Signs
summary: Short Stuff episode on hobo signs. Josh and Chuck open by distinguishing hobo, tramp, and bum (per the NSA's account citing hoboes): a hobo travels to work and works to travel, a tramp travels but doesn't like to work, and a bum neither travels nor works. They run through competing theories for the origin of the word "hobo" (hoe boy, homeward bound, hello boy/low boy, homo bonus). They then describe hobo signs: temporary chalk marks left for other hobos about town conditions such as free meals, dangerous houses, doctors who don't charge, and bad-tempered householders. Examples include a top hat (wealthy resident), a cross (religious talk gets a meal), a chicken (free use of the telephone), and three diagonal lines (unsafe). They note the Historical Graffiti Society doubts a codified system ever existed, with media fascination with hobo literature as a possible source, and that documented hobo marks were usually a direction letter, nickname, and date. They mention John Hodgman's roughly 800 invented hobo names, and close with "war chalking," the early-2000s practice of marking locations with open Wi-Fi.

segments.title: Hobo, tramp, and bum definitions
segments.summary: Josh introduces the episode and explains the NSA's account, citing hoboes, of the differences between a hobo, a tramp, and a bum.

segments.title: Origin of the word hobo
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh weigh several theories for the origin of the word hobo: hoe boy, homeward bound, hello boy becoming low boy, and the Latin homo bonus. They dismiss most as unlikely.

segments.title: Setting up hobo signs
segments.summary: Josh explains that hobos left signs for one another with information about towns, such as where to get a free meal or which house to avoid, and that these developed into a codified system.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break before the discussion of sign meanings.

segments.title: Why signs were temporary and the meaning of common symbols
segments.summary: Chuck explains that signs were temporary because conditions changed. Hosts discuss the top hat, train engine, and cross symbols, plus the George Washington and horse anecdote from Gilbert Stewart.

segments.title: Confusing and dubious symbols
segments.summary: Hosts go through symbols whose meanings are not intuitive: chicken (free telephone), camping spot, sideways cross with three dots (doctor who does not charge), circle and square with a dot (bad temper), and three diagonal lines (unsafe).

segments.title: Doubts about a codified system
segments.summary: Josh says the origin of the signs is unknown. The Historical Graffiti Society, as profiled by Atlas Obscura, has found no evidence of the roughly fifty codified signs and suspects media fascination created them. Documented real marks were direction letters, nicknames, and dates.

segments.title: John Hodgman's hobo names
segments.summary: Chuck mentions John Hodgman's book with roughly 800 invented hobo names and reads a few examples. Hosts joke about people asking him for hobo names.

segments.title: War chalking and early Wi-Fi
segments.summary: Josh describes war chalking in the early 2000s, when hobo-like marks showed where open Wi-Fi could be found. The practice faded as routers were secured, while free Wi-Fi zones grew in cities.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck close the episode and note the show is an iHeartRadio production.
